extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, sculptors, painters, and other artists or critics working in tragic art and the depiction of the sublime/pathos
extracted.subtask_short: writing tragic art and the sublime
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive aesthetic guidance for creating works of the sublime and the pathetic, especially tragic art: how to represent suffering, moral resistance, and the relation between sensuous impressions and reason. Emphasises techniques, anti-patterns, and aims for elevating the spectator from sense to the super-sensuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime as a mixed feeling revealing moral independence
rubrics_metrics.description: "The feeling of the sublime is a mixed feeling. It is at once a painful state...and a joyous state..." — the sublime unites two contrary sensations and thereby proves our moral independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain and evoke how the sublime combines pain (awareness of limits) and a higher joy (rapture) that shows the spirit's autonomy. Use scenes/objects that simultaneously provoke shudder and exaltation so the audience experiences the separation between sensuous instincts and reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show the sublime as reason's triumph over sensuous limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: "In presence of the sublime we feel ourselves sublime, because the sensuous instincts have no influence over the jurisdiction of reason...it is then the pure spirit that acts in us..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present objects or situations that overwhelm the imagination or the senses but allow the mind to 'attain by thought' what senses cannot. Make clear that what elevates is the spectator's thought/resistance, not mere sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the terrible or overwhelming to point beyond sensuous nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The sublime object may be considered... we either represent it to our comprehension... or we refer it to our vital force, and we consider it as a power before which ours is nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include vistas of magnitude, terror, or incomprehensibility (vast oceans, heights beyond vision, destructive nature) to push the spectator from sensuous reaction toward contemplation of the supersensuous ideal. The attraction to such objects must be framed as intellectual/spiritual, not only sensory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should imitate appearance, not reality (freeing art from nature's shackles)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Art...is fully free, because it throws off all accidental restrictions and leaves the mind free, because it imitates the appearance, not the reality of objects."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing, focus on the appearance that best communicates the sublime/pathos rather than slavishly reproducing external realism. Select, emphasize, or omit details (accidentals) to make the essential (the necessary expression of the soul) clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic art's ultimate aim: represent the super-sensuous
rubrics_metrics.description: "The highest aim of art is to represent the super-sensuous, and this is effected in particular by tragic art..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that tragic works lead the audience beyond mere feeling to an awareness of the moral/spiritual (reason). All depictions of suffering should serve this higher aim rather than being ends in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: First law of tragic art: depict suffering nature with vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: "The pathetic is the first condition required most strictly in a tragic author...He must give in some sort to his hero, as to his reader, their full load of suffering..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the sensuous, suffering aspects of characters convincing and intense so the subsequent demonstration of moral resistance will be meaningful. Do not underplay physical/emotional pain if it is required to set up moral dilemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second law of tragic art: show moral resistance to suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: "The second law is to represent the resistance of morality opposed to suffering."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always pair vivid suffering with evidence of a super-sensuous principle—will, conscience, reason—resisting or transcending that suffering. The aesthetic value of pathos depends on its being shown as met and resisted by moral freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathetic has value only insofar as it is sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: "The pathetic only has aesthetic value in as far as it is sublime."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating pathos as merely emotive or sentimental. Only when suffering points to reason or moral greatness (the sublime) does it become worthy of tragic art. Evaluate scenes by whether they move the audience toward the idea of the super-sensuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid soft tenderness and sentimentalism (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The soft emotions...are of the nature of the agreeable, with which the fine arts are not concerned...The only effect of these works is to empty the lachrymal duct, and soothe the overflowing feelings; but the mind comes back from them empty."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not aim merely to elicit tears or soothing tenderness. Scenes that only produce languid, agreeable emotion without strengthening the moral/ intellectual life of the audience are beneath tragic art. Prefer situations that challenge and elevate rather than merely console.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject extreme affections that crush moral freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Real taste excludes all extreme affections...These affections oppress moral liberty by pain...they can excite aversion, and not the emotion that would alone be worthy of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of depicting passions in degrees so extreme that the character's intelligence is extinguished; such portrayals negate the possibility of moral resistance and thus fail aesthetically. Maintain balance so suffering shows resistance, not annihilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid decorum and icy declamation that falsify nature (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: The icy tone of declamation extinguishes all nature...the French tragedians...make it quite impossible for them to paint human nature truly. Decorum...always falsifies the expression of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not sacrifice genuine natural expression for rigid rules of propriety, rhetoric, or rank. Avoid stilted, self-conscious declamation; allow characters to feel and speak in ways that reveal authentic suffering and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model the Greek approach: show the human (necessary) not the accidental
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greek artist...sets aside the drapery, and shows us nude figures...This is because drapery is to him an accidental thing, and because the necessary ought never to be sacrificed to the accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strip away extraneous status markers or decorum when they conceal the human reality. Emphasize universal human responses (the necessary) rather than social rank or costume when you wish to convey pathos and moral strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make moral greatness evident by its persistence after change
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man who was virtuous in prosperity remains so in adversity...his virtue could not be explained by any reason drawn from the physical order...We must...seek the principle of his conduct in quite another world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct character and plot so that moral qualities persist under reversed circumstances, demonstrating that the principle of action is beyond sensuous causes. Use contrast (prosperity vs. misfortune) to reveal genuine virtue as non-sensuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent the super-sensuous indirectly via phenomena inexplicable by sense
rubrics_metrics.description: All phenomena of which the ultimate principle cannot be derived from the world of sense are an indirect representation of the upper-sensuous element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since pure ideas cannot be directly depicted, select or stage sensuous phenomena whose causes cannot plausibly be rooted entirely in natural/physical explanations, so they suggest an intelligible, moral, or spiritual principle behind them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the hero plausibly sensuous before elevating him to reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero of tragedy must first have justified his claim to be a sensuous being before aspiring to our homage as a reasonable being...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish the character's bodily desires and sensuous responses convincingly so that when he displays moral steadfastness, the audience recognizes it as an act of reason rather than mere absence of passion. The credibility of moral resistance depends on an earlier, persuasive presentation of sensuousity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use familiar tragic/pathos imagery to fortify audience against misfortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever passes in review the terrible fate of Mithridates, of Syracuse, and Carthage, cannot help keeping his appetite in check...The capacity of the sublime is one of the noblest aptitudes of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include historical or mythic examples of suffering and downfall to habituate and strengthen the spectator's spirit; pathos practiced in art can prepare minds to face real misfortune and turn it into a sublime experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate instinctive/animal reactions from willful resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: There are phenomena connected simply with animal nature...and other organs...subject to the will...the contest with affection presupposes something that is distinct from sensuous nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In depiction, avoid conflating involuntary, instinctive reactions with moral agency. Make visible which actions are instinctive and which are the result of deliberate, rational resistance; the latter is what creates pathos worthy of art.
